newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia sounds tough note after Yeltsin-Kohl talks.
newsitem.headline: Russia sounds tough note after Yeltsin-Kohl talks.

text.p: The Kremlin is prepared to discuss relations with NATO but remains firmly opposed to the western defence alliance's plans to expand eastwards, President Boris Yeltsin's spokesman said on Sunday.
The comments by Sergei Yastrzembsky dampened the optimism expressed by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl after weekend talks with Yeltsin.

Kohl, the first western leader to see Yeltsin since his heart operation, said after the meeting that it might be possible to solve differences with the Russians over NATO enlargement this year, but Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had not softened his opposition to the alliance's expansion plans.

"There is a well known divergence in Russia's position on one hand and Germany and the other members of the North Atlantic alliance on the other on these issues (NATO expansion)," Yastrzhembsky told Interfax news agency.
"Boris Yeltsin clearly, precisely and fairly toughly laid out Russia's position and concern about the consequences of possible NATO expansion to the East," he added.
Yastrzembsky also repeated a statement made after the talks, that the two leaders had agreed to continue negotiations and contacts on the theme of Russia-NATO.
Kohl had sounded a more upbeat note at a news conference after his Saturday meeting with Yeltsin at the Rus hunting lodge, some 100 km (60 miles) west of Moscow.
"There are still some differences of opinion," he said. "But we evaluated a couple of ideas which I will discuss with my NATO colleagues over the next couple of days on the telephone.
"The mistrust from the era of the Cold War must go. I see a good chance and this chance has to be taken up now and in the coming months," he added, saying it would need much negotiation.

NATO foreign ministers agreed last month to issue invitations in July for the first former Soviet bloc countries to join the alliance, and at the same time offer Russia a role in shaping Europe's defence arrangements.
But Moscow has vehemently opposed NATO's expansion plans, seeing them as a threat to its security and as a humiliating confirmation of its loss of superpower status.
Lacking the diplomatic sway to veto the expansion, Russian ministers and officials have adopted a confusing mix of tough and conciliatory language.
Many western analysts explain the mixed signals by saying that Russia has reconciled itself to the first wave of NATO enlargement but is taking a tough position in order to secure other concessions.
